name: The Centre Holds
consequence: Your middle stands firm. Your wings give ground.
blurb: Put your best men in the middle and tell them not to move. The edges of the line will bend — that is the price, and you pay it on purpose.
evidence: The king and his guard stood in the centre of an Achaemenid line, and Greek accounts of Cunaxa and Gaugamela describe a Persian centre that held while the wings gave way. Concentrating strength somewhere means thinning it somewhere else.
disputed: That the centre was deliberately reinforced at the expense of the wings is an inference from where the king stood, not a recorded doctrine.

name: Shoot the Horses
consequence: Every archer you have shoots at riders first, whatever else is closer.
blurb: A rider on foot is just a man. Ignore the infantry walking at you and put every arrow into the horses — then deal with what is left.
evidence: Bringing down the mount rather than the rider is the standard answer to cavalry across the ancient world, and it is a choice with a cost: while the archers are shooting at the wings, nothing is shooting at what is coming up the middle.
disputed: Target priority is a game abstraction. No ancient source describes an Achaemenid rule for what archers shot at first.

name: Broken Ground
consequence: Your whole army fights better in a pass, and worse on open plain.
blurb: Learn to fight where there is no room. It will win you a gorge and lose you a field, so look at the ground before you take this.
evidence: Ariobarzanes held the Persian Gates against Alexander with a small force precisely because the ground took away everything a larger army could do with it. Troops trained for close country pay for it wherever the country is open.
disputed: The Persian Gates action is attested; a standing doctrine of training for broken country is not. This card generalises one engagement into a choice.
